title: Loose Rein plan.yaml (rein-grounded-v1)
description: The Expected Model: what this cycle claims the implementation will do, and the task DAG that builds it. Frozen with the mandate. Three sections and no more — `claims` ties each R-N/NFR-N heading of docs/10-requirements.md to a statement, `tasks` ties each statement to the work that answers it, and `rein dag --trace` walks the thread end to end. Every enum here is mirrored by a constant in rein/models.py; tests/test_models.py fails if the two drift.

scope.description: What the loop may change under this mandate. Each entry covers the path it names and everything beneath it; a trailing '/' is optional punctuation, and the prefix is anchored at a separator (`src/app` covers `src/app/x.py`, never `src/app.py`). An empty `include` is unbounded — every guarded path is in scope — which is the honest default for a cycle that has not narrowed itself, and is what the five phase gates amounted to once the last of them opened. `rein guard` refuses a write outside it, so this is the mechanical half of "the range you may delegate".

decisions.description: Every decision the drafting phase met, with who settled it. The list a human reads at the mandate gate is not what they were asked — it is what they were *not* asked: each `local` entry is a default the loop took on its own reading of the reach, and the gate is where that reading is overruled while overruling it is still cheap.

lenses.description: The review lenses this cycle applies, frozen with the mandate. Written by `rein lens --select` while the plan is still a draft and read back by it afterwards, so the reviewer at the code stage is handed the same set the gate screen showed.

repoPath.description: A repo-relative POSIX path. Checked for what it must not be rather than for which characters it may contain: no absolute form, no `..` segment, no empty segment, no backslash, no control character. It was an ASCII allow-list, which rejected `app/[[...path]]/page.tsx`, `app/(group)/`, and every non-ASCII filename — a reference to real code read as an attempt to escape the repository. What the rule is actually about is escaping, and that is what it now says. A leading `-` is refused as well, which is not about escaping: a path that begins with one can be read as an option by any command it is handed to, and refusing it here covers every call site at once.

claim.description: What one requirement means, in a sentence a reviewer can hold against the code. `requirement_ids` is what makes it traceable: a claim citing an id no heading declares is a dangling reference, and a heading no claim cites is an uncovered requirement — `rein dag --trace` blocks on both.

kind.description: The DAG role that drives orchestration: layers, parallelism, and merge order derive from it, not from LLM discretion.

scope.description: Where this task's work belongs. Each entry covers the path it names and everything beneath it; a trailing '/' is optional punctuation and changes nothing, and the prefix is anchored at a separator (`src/app` covers `src/app/x.py`, never `src/app.py`). An empty `include` is unbounded, not forbidden. Checked against the real diff by the build loop.

acceptance.description: This task's own bar, in a form something can check. Acceptance criteria used to live only as markdown checkboxes in `docs/tasks/T-NNN.md`, which nothing parsed — so 'the acceptance criteria are met' was an assertion by the agent that wrote the code. Stating them here does NOT let a task pick its own quality gate: the shared DoD in config.yaml still runs, unchanged, and this list is frozen by a human at the mandate exactly like everything else in the plan.

operator_surface.description: What this task will require of a person: a setting somebody has to supply, a schema somebody has to migrate, a dependency somebody has to provide, a signal somebody has to watch. Frozen with the mandate along with the rest of the task, which is what turns it into an Expected side — at acceptance the blind extractor's readings are sorted by whether one of these foresaw them, and the readings nothing foresaw are what the approver is shown first. Declaring nothing is allowed; it means every operator-facing reading in that area arrives at acceptance as undeclared.

kind.description: A subset of the Actual Statement categories in review.schema.json, not a vocabulary of its own: the declaration is compared against what a blind extractor read out of the code, and two vocabularies over one comparison would need a mapping table that can be wrong. These are the categories describing a surface somebody outside the code can see.

name.description: What a person deals with, in their words — a settings key, a table and column, a queue, an endpoint. Never matched against anything: prose compared to prose is the overclaim the acceptance brief exists to avoid, so `paths` is what carries the comparison.

paths.description: Where this surface can be read at the reviewed commit — the migration, the schema file, the settings module. Covered the same way `scope` is (the path it names and everything beneath it, trailing slash optional), and this is what an extracted statement's code anchor is matched against. It is also what acceptance offers as the as-built view: the file as it ends up, which a diff never shows.

reversible.description: Whether this surface can be taken back once the task that creates it has run. Not a new question: the architect answers it for every requirement and the design carries it into the task, which is where `/tasks` reads it from — it was simply dropped on the way into this record, leaving the answer in prose that only the acceptance brief opens, after the thing has happened. Required and boolean, with no default, because an omitted answer used to read as `true` by silence. `false` makes the task an irreversible point: the cycle gains a gate named for it and the loop stops there before running it, which is the only place the answer can still change anything.

adr.description: The decision record that settled what this requires of a person and whether it can be undone. Shown beside the declaration at acceptance so the trade-off a human approved with the mandate is reachable from what was built — the review never restates it, because a restatement is a sentence nobody observed.

statement.description: One criterion, stated so that it could be false.

evidence.description: How this criterion is established. Absent means it is prose only — most criteria are, and that is honest; it simply contributes no evidence and is left to the acceptance review.

kind.description: `command` runs an argv in a sandboxed profile and is decided by exit status. `artifact` requires the named paths to exist. `external` is evidence this loop cannot obtain — a staging check, a device, a person — so a task carrying one reaches `awaiting-evidence` rather than `done`, and a human records the observation with `rein evidence record`.

command.description: An argv array, never a shell string — the same rule the quality gate follows, for the same reason.

decision.description:
One thing that had to be settled before the loop could build, and how it was settled. `reach` is the criterion that decides who settles it: a decision whose reversal would collapse the scope is `mandate` and a human settles it before the gate; one whose reversal stays local is `local` and the loop settles it and records it here. Asking about every default the loop would otherwise take is the wider net and it spends the drafting phase; asking about what cannot be undone locally is the one that pays. `status: unknown` is the honest answer when nobody has one — recorded rather than filled in with a default, and never turned into a claim, because a claim nothing can make true cannot be judged. A `mandate` decision left `unknown` is what `rein approve mandate` refuses: the scope is not yet defined enough to delegate.

Three conditional requirements, because the gate screen is built out of these fields and a field nothing requires is a screen that can go silently blank. A `settled` decision must name `settled_by`: the list a human reads at the gate is every decision the *loop* settled, so an omitted `settled_by` would drop an entry from the one list the record exists to produce. An `unknown` decision must *not* carry one, because nobody settled it. And a `local` decision must carry a `rationale`: the reach claim is that reversing it later costs one task, and the rationale is the only material a human has for overruling that claim.

rationale.description: Why this reach. Required for `local` (see the conditional requirements above): the claim being made is that reversing it later costs one task, and that claim is the thing a human overrules at the gate.

settled_by.description: Who settled it. Required when `status` is `settled`, forbidden when it is `unknown`. What it separates is a default the loop took from a default a human looked at and kept: both read as settled afterwards, and only the first is a thing the gate shows.

lensSelection.description: One lens this cycle's review will use, resolved against this plan and frozen with it. The library the ids come from is user-global and mutable; this list is not. Without it a review's inputs would be a function of whatever `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/rein/lenses.yaml` happened to say when the reviewer ran — the same repository would be reviewed differently on another laptop, or after one line of an overlay changed, with nothing in the audit chain to show it. `status: applied` is a lens whose condition the machine settled; `proposed` is one a human keeps or drops at the gate, recorded because dropping it is a decision.
